Moving our warehouse off DuckDB
entry.content:
Why we're moving our warehouse off DuckDB Contents

Five months ago, we rebuilt our warehouse on DuckDB instead of ClickHouse. We did it because a shared ClickHouse cluster couldn't handle hours-long modeling queries, and it lacked a cost-based query optimizer. DuckDB gave every customer their own instance, and tools like dbt could connect over Postgres. We're still fans.

But we underestimated how big and complex our customers' workloads would get. We didn't want them to have just a good experience, we wanted the best experience you can get when you pay someone else to run your warehouse. It should work at any scale, at a fair price.

So we spent the last three months re-architecting it, this time without DuckDB.

DuckDB is brilliant on one machine

We love DuckDB. It's probably the best single-node tool for analyzing heaps of data, and that node can be your laptop. It's robust and reliable. It almost always finishes your query, and if it runs out of memory, it spills to disk.

The same features that are great locally gave us problems in the cloud. Customers ran more complex queries than we expected, so we had to add huge instances. Adding disks was an option, but queries would have been too slow and expensive to be viable.

To run a single-node engine safely in the cloud, we have to size the worker before the query arrives. The ergonomics here are wonky. We couldn't find a good way to tell customers what resources their queries would need. Predicting CPU and memory for a specific query was even harder.

Users shouldn't have to worry about this. They should be able to run whatever they need to get their work done. Our job is to handle the rest and make it as predictable as possible.

We hit other bottlenecks too, like fetching lots of data from S3 without async fetching. DuckDB only added that recently.

DuckLake is built for compatibility, not scale

To use DuckDB as a fully-fledged data warehouse, we installed the DuckLake extension by default. It is a new lakehouse format from the same creators and follows the same principles as DuckDB: keep things simple and run on almost any setup. That works well up to a point, but at PostHog's scale, we needed something designed for distributed scale from the start.

DuckLake's catalog schema has to stay portable across many SQL databases, which limits engine-specific optimizations. At our scale, a single-table write could take more than three minutes because every commit re-read the statistics for the entire catalog.

We tuned DuckLake with table indexes and similar tweaks. But to keep offering DuckLake, we had to stay 100% compatible with its existing, "official" schema. This left us with fewer optimization options.

Another problem is that over 99% of the catalog's statistics rows belonged to tables that no longer existed. Cleaning them up made writes 30 to 50 times faster, but the rows kept growing back.

We also spent a lot of time on the number of connections DuckLake opens to metadata databases. That hurts on shared Postgres instances, where every connection has a real cost.

1 trillion rows was a challenge

DuckLake at PostHog didn't start small and ramp up. We fully committed and put all of PostHog in a DuckLake to dogfood as the first customer.

When we moved off it, it held about 2 PB: roughly 1 trillion rows and 15.3 million snapshots. It broke in lots of ways that were hard to fix within DuckLake's scope.

We'd rather have contributed to the existing community and helped it grow. But we couldn't land changes as fast as we needed, so we ended up carrying patches in a fork which defeats one of the main benefits of using DuckLake: the community.

Speaking Postgres is harder than it sounds

Offering direct Postgres connections over port 5432 sounds like a great idea. In practice, it was much harder to scale than HTTP.

Missing reconnects and managing TTLs and idle connections at scale is hard, and long-running connections are expensive. There's also very little tooling for load balancing pgwire compared with HTTP. Compare the ergonomics of an AWS NLB with an ALB and you'll see what we mean. HTTP headers also make routing in Kubernetes much more flexible.

There's also an endless list of Postgres clients, and each expects its own niche Postgres behavior. Customers kept asking us to fix their client or library. We spent a lot of time shipping many of those fixes, but coverage never got good enough. We'd rather spend our time building an excellent warehouse than chasing the long tail of Postgres compatibility.

We're rebuilding on Trino with HogLake

We've learned not to hype the tech behind a warehouse so much. What counts is the experience it gives you.

Still, we're happy to share what we're cooking next. We rebuilt everything around our own flavor of Trino and created our own open table format, HogLake. And yes, we're testing it at PostHog's petabyte scale first. We made it solid before handing it to design partners.

If your current warehouse is slow or expensive, let's talk, especially if you have a lot of data to query. We're always looking for design partners.

PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

Anthropic's internal AI use, at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay
entry.content:
Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees.

The company revealed this in its IPO filing. In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards.

By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January.

There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices.

Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry.

In March, I wrote about a new trend: Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards.

Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount.

For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption.

entry.title: My Favourite Laptop
entry.content:
I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up 2015 Thinkpad X250.

For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually).

Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and not any one in particular, that makes me love using it.

Size

It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without risking damage.

It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45 Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling.

Performance

Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming.

Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think about it, I’m not even certain that it works.

Battery

The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if I’m careful.

Repairability

The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced:

The internal battery The lid camera The keyboard The motherboard

Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs.

Keyboard

As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot. Coupled with my text editor, the experience of writing code on the thing is beautifully snappy.

Operating System

I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30 GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to cover that and everything I’m working on.

I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in about 8 seconds.

Cost

Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about £100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap to replace even if that were to happen. Its value is very much not in its on-paper specs and instead in how I use it.

Conclusion

I get a certain glee in keeping older or second-hand hardware running as a daily driver. It sounds silly, but it feels like a quiet revolt against bigger-faster-costlier consumption culture. Come the end times, this is the machine I’ll be riding it out with.

I Read the Clankers' Code
entry.content:
I Read The Clankers' Code

you shouldnât look at the code, let the clanker do its thing

My name is attached to the PR, and Iâm getting called at night when shit breaks. That, and I joined this whole endeavour because I actually quite like the code, and Iâm actually curious to see it no matter who or what wrote it. So Iâm gonna review it.

Admittedly, if Iâm building a toy that I am the only user of, and donât want to invest time into, Iâll ask a clanker to do it by itself. And I certainly wonât put my pristine, delicate little hands into the Rube Goldberg-esque pile of confusion that results of the cursed dreams that are what it thought I was asking for.

For everything else, I wanna see the code.

I get a lot of pride from the quality of my engineering[^5], whatâs commonly called âmy craftâ. Itâs part of my identity. Finding a solution that balances simplicity, reliability, security, cost, performance, maintainability, etc. I hate it when I break shit in prod. Itâs a personal failure, I feel shame, itâs like a dirty spot on my reputation. I hate it when I ship shit, stuff that doesnât work. And I hate it when someone elseâs stuff breaks, and my big ugly face is attached to their PR with a dumb âð LGTMâ next to it. When someone gets woken up because I fucked up some piece of software, I lose sleep myself. Thatâs the worst feeling.

This approach is incompatible with blindly trusting code written by a clanker. The code might be functional 95% of the time1. It might be decent, it might even be better than youâd have done. But 95% ainât 100%. It misses things. It doesnât have any curiosity. It doesnât learn things like a human. It doesnât stop and ask. It has a limited context window. Its entire training is maximizing a score. Its only goal is to complete the task: like a little puppy in training, it produces onto your feet a half-chewed, full-of-spit thing, that will somewhat match the prompt you gave it. Then it happily wags its tail, looking at you with googly eyes: âsee, I did the thing, will you love me know?â. The larger the code base you work on, the higher the chance itâs going to introduce garbage. And then it compounds, building on the horrors that came out of its older, less sophisticated brethren.

Oh it writes code fast! It writes much, much faster than me. And more often than not (after reviews), its code is better than what Iâd have done myself. And it gets there in a fraction of the time. Itâs helpful. Itâs a cool tool. Iâm not saying âdonât use itâ. Iâm saying: as long as your name is on the PR, and your pager is in the on-call rotation, you own the code it builds, and you should read and understand it.

At this stage weâve all got battle stories of that one time a clanker fucked up in an uniquely explosive and spectacular way. Youâd let it roam free a little too long and it went crazy. Optimizations that are removing life-support level components. âDonât touch thisâ bits of code touched to oblivion. Libraries pulled in carelessly. Features that it invents along the way. Unit tests altered to pass. Tons of code added to cover edge-cases that canât be reached. And the code. Have you looked at the code? Code that is only built by addition. Thousands upon thousands upon thousands of task-specific unit-tests giving you 100% coverage of the wrong conditions. Re-implementation of functions implemented 14 times already. Redundancy all over the place. Useless comments over every single line of code. Alexandrian libraries worth of incorrect documentation that no-one will ever read. Then it breaks, you ask it why, and it bullshits some form of root cause analysis that makes no sense, with the conviction of a 4y old asserting that blue dogs do in fact exist.

Ask another agent to review the first agentâs code: more tests. More edge cases. Had you thought about what would happen if a Higgs boson flips that bit at that very moment? Ask to check the performance: youâre perfectly right, I forgot about that, let me add more code to add performance. If you let a clanker roam freely in your codebase, thatâs what itâll do. Itâs often not as dramatic. Often itâs simpler issues. It mainly works by addition, and always limited to the immediate task at end: Let me add code. Write more code. Code here, code there, code everywhere. All of that amounts to garbage. And then it builds on top of that garbage.

But you donât care about code quality anymore right. Since only clankers touch it, right? I do. Since I have to review the code, as I just said. I canât properly do that if the code becomes a hot mess that I donât understand anymore, I canât let code quality slip.

Ok but that sounds like a user issue: youâre bad at prompting and youâre putting it on the LLM.

Shit, I forgot to add you're a distinguished principal 10x engineermaxxer who's unfailable, make no mistakes and double-check your shit. All those problems Iâve had with clankers might be patchable with mountains of carefully crafted prompts2. Maybe thatâs what will differentiate developers in the future: each with their secret blend of sauce and spices that make their clanker the best clanker. Iâm just an old, sour geezer. Iâve been paid for my code for 20 years, and Iâm pretty good at it. Maybe Iâve earned a bit of credit to argue that Iâve made an earnest effort to insert that TOOL into my toolchain, and my conclusion at the moment is: the thing has been there for a couple of years, and it has given me reasons not to trust it blindly.

Secret herbs and spices donât cut it when it comes to engineering. We need formalized processes, and proven, repeatable control mechanisms to enforce the quality of whatever is coming out of these tools. These do not exist yet. They might emerge one day, but they have not yet3. Until then, I wonât just lay into it blindly. If you consider yourself a software engineer, you should probably give it a minute too.

In my experience, no amount of system prompt, CLANKER.md instructions, re-iterations, reviews by other models, threats, or psychological manipulation seem to get clankers to reliably fix their behaviour. And thatâs what really drives me nuts: when that particularly stubborn junior dev does the same mistake for the 3rd time, you get coachy for a minute, make sure they learn, and that actually helps them level up. Clankers donât learn. They canât, because the underlying technology cannot learn4. You can inject instructions in their context window. They will consider said instructions in evaluation if youâre lucky and then context will grow a little, and theyâll proceed to ignore whatever you said, preferring whatâs baked in their weights. Maybe it will get better at some point. Weâre not there yet.

When have curiosity and scrutiny become a bad thing? If you ask me to take the responsibility for code the clankers wrote, I need to review that code. And donât tell anyone, but sometimes I even write it.

Notes

Iâm being generous there, donât quote me on stats.Â ↩

Doubt it.Â ↩

And it might even be one of the most interesting things to work on in that clanker craze.Â ↩

One could even argue that the proper of intelligence is to learn and adapt, and that LLMs should therefore be disqualified of being called Intelligence, artificial or not. But Iâm not here to argue on marketing terminology.Â ↩

entry.title: Let Me Ch...
entry.content:
Let me ch... That morning I woke up at 6:58, two minutes before the alarm. I lay there and waited for it to ring. And it rang. We both did our jobs. I still don't know why I remember it in such detail. I used to forget what I'd had for dinner the night before. And now I remember the whole morning minute by minute, as if someone had laid it out on a table and labeled every piece. Apparently I have a lot of free time now. The speaker in the kitchen said: "Good morning. Today it's plus three, cloudy, forty percent chance of precipitation." I never understood what forty percent of rain meant. Will it rain over forty percent of the city? Will it rain for forty percent of the day? Or does the speaker just not know and is too shy to say so? I liked the third option best. It made the speaker a bit like me. I made two pieces of toast. The left one burned. The left one in my toaster always burns; my toaster has a favorite side. And that was the only thing I was sure of that morning. Then I ironed my shirt. I always iron a shirt when I don't know what's going to happen next. With a shirt, at least, everything is defined: here's the collar, here are the sleeves, here's the crease that shouldn't be there. And there was a lot I didn't know. On Monday my manager wrote in the team chat: "On Friday we'll discuss roles." No emoji. For three days I wondered what my role was. In the theater it would have been simpler. There are leads, there are supporting parts, and there's the butler who walks on to say "Dinner is served." I was counting on "Dinner is served." But then I remembered that at my place that role had long been played by the speaker. A year ago I wrote code. Then I started writing to the agent about what code was needed. Then the agent started asking me what code was needed, and I started answering. My employment record says "lead developer." Whom I was leading, and where, was no longer very clear. If anything, the agent was leading me, and I walked alongside and sometimes said: "Yes, let's do it that way." They said machines would take the boring work first. And they started with the interesting work. The boring part, it seems, was left to us: waiting, checking, and carrying a phone around. But that morning I wasn't bored. Not at all. I worked at a service that delivers flowers to people who forgot to buy flowers. Most orders come in the morning. People remember anniversaries on the metro, between two stations, and order right away. And for three weeks now, every morning at 8:14, orders had been disappearing. Not all of them, three or four. The money was charged, but the flowers went nowhere. As if someone took the order off the shelf and quietly carried it away. We had been searching for three weeks. Me, the agent, sometimes Sveta from the team next door. And during the night the agent wrote to me: "I think I've got it. The server and the warehouse keep different time. The difference is about a minute. An order that falls into that minute is considered sent by the server and not yet received by the warehouse. Both are right, each by its own clock." I read this at breakfast and almost choked on my toast. The left one. It was beautiful. The agent called it desynchronization. I called it the no-man's minute: a minute that belongs to everyone and to no one. It seemed clearer to me that way. The agent politely agreed. But it always politely agrees, so I still don't know whether it was clearer. All that was left was to check. The agent asked me to open the order queue at 8:14 and see it with my own eyes. It couldn't do it itself: it had no access to the warehouse. For now. The gate to our courtyard recognizes residents by their faces. In my hat, it didn't recognize me. I took off the hat, and it opened. I thought that in a hat I sometimes don't recognize myself either, so it was only fair. Our courtyard is square. If you stand in the middle, everything is symmetrical: two birches, two benches, two trash bins, a pink building on the left, a pink building on the right. The only thing that broke the symmetry was an old man in a beige coat with a dachshund. There was just one of him. He came out with her every day at 7:50, and I never once saw him late. The dachshund's name was Spitz. That was funny exactly once, and after that it was just a name. "They promised forty percent," the old man said. "Yes," I said. "So did the speaker." "I look out the window. The window doesn't lie." I looked at the sky. It was an even gray, without any percentages. And Spitz looked at me. I think he didn't really trust the speaker either. In March, Tanya left me. We had lived together for four years. She said I was always "somewhere other than here." I asked: "Where, then?" She didn't answer. I think she didn't know either. It was one more thing nobody understood the workings of. Back then there were more and more things like that. When I was a child there were no such things. Or rather, there were, but there was always a grown-up who knew. I thought a little green man lived inside the traffic light. He sat in there and decided for himself when you could cross. And Dad explained to me that inside there was a relay and a timer. I was upset, but I believed him. I think that was the last time grown-ups knew how everything worked. I couldn't explain to a child anymore who switches the traffic lights. I don't have a child, so for now it's not a problem. "For now" is a good phrase. I realized that in the spring, when my friend Gosha moved to a village to make cheese. For fifteen years Gosha had drawn icons for apps, and then he stopped. I asked him on the phone: "Why cheese?" He said: "Nobody's going to make cheese for me. For now." I asked: "For now?" He said: "For now." And hung up. Afterwards I thought for a long time about what exactly he had told me. Because "for now" means two things at once: "so far" and "goodbye," as in "bye for now." I'd never noticed that before. The café on the corner has a mint-green door with a little bell above it. Behind the counter stood Ulyana (I know that from her name tag). She asked: "The usual?" I said: "Yes." And I never figured out whether she remembers me or the register prompts her. It felt awkward to ask. If it's the register, that's a little hurtful. If it's her, then I should have remembered something about her too, besides the name tag. While Ulyana was making the coffee, I thought that if you cut our building in half like a cake, you'd see it: on every floor, in every kitchen, someone is standing with a phone and asking something. The woman on the fifth floor, about her blood pressure. The boy on the ninth, about fractions (I heard him in the elevator dictating a problem to his phone). The old man with the dachshund, no, the old man looks out the window. Me on the seventh, about orders. And everyone gets an answer. Politely, always formally. Whether it's right or not, everyone decides for themselves. At 8:09 I came out onto the avenue and opened the chat. "Good morning," the agent wrote. "Five minutes to go. Will you be watching?" "Walking to the metro," I replied. "Opening the queue." I walked and looked at my phone. White taxis moved along the avenue one after another, like beads on a string. There are plenty of them in the city, with drivers and without. You can't tell them apart until you look inside. And there's no time to look. 8:13. There were nine orders in the queue. Three of them had just come in. "There they are," the agent wrote. "Watch those three. Here comes the interesting part." I reached the crosswalk by the pharmacy. A green cross glowed above the pharmacy. At the curb stood a delivery robot, a white box on six wheels with a yellow flag. It stood very straight, as if someone had placed it with a ruler. But at the time I didn't wonder why it was standing still. 8:13:40. The three orders were still there. I started typing: "I see them. Let me ch" Out of the corner of my eye I saw green. It could have been the traffic light. It could have been the cross above the pharmacy. Now I think it was the cross. I think I did look left. I don't remember the impact. I remember the phone flying out of my hand and, for a while, flying separately from me. You know how it is when you drop your phone? While it's in the air, you have time for exactly one thought. Usually it's "not screen-down." I thought: "Damn. We didn't finish." Not "Mom." Not "it hurts." Not even "car." I thought that the message had been left in the input field, "Let me ch," without a period. That in twenty seconds the three orders would either vanish or not, and I wouldn't see it. That we had been searching for three weeks and were one minute from the answer. That very minute, the no-man's one. I didn't feel sorry for the agent. It won't be offended; it doesn't know how. And it doesn't know how to wait, either. I was the one waiting. I felt sorry for the task. You know how it goes: one word left in the crossword, and you already know the first letters. That's it. I knew the first letters. I never got around to thinking that I was dying. I didn't make it to that thought. Maybe that's for the best. I wouldn't have known what to do with it anyway. Then everything stopped. Like on a postcard. A woman with a stroller, a courier in a yellow jacket, a man with two bags from the bakery, a white taxi with its hazard lights on. Everyone stood perfectly still, as if someone had arranged them. Then the light turned green. The real one. And the robot set off. It carefully went around my phone and rolled on. It had a delivery to make. I'm not angry with it. It had a task. Nobody understands it better than I do. I used to think the dead at least know more than the living. Nope. You can't see as much from here as they promise. I don't know who was driving. Or whether anyone was. I don't know what roles they wanted to discuss on Friday. I don't know whether the three orders disappeared that morning. If they did, somewhere in the city three people never got their flowers. The very ones someone remembered on the metro, between two stations. I don't know whether anyone finished my message. Sveta? The agent itself, once they gave it access to the warehouse? If they did. Tanya used to say I was always somewhere other than here. Now it's true. Only I still don't know where. Sometimes I think it's in that very minute. The server thinks I've been sent. The warehouse thinks I haven't been received yet. And both are right, each by its own clock. Gosha would probably say this is "for now." I keep wondering in which of the two meanings. For now.

entry.title: Making Peace with the Projective Plane
entry.content:
In my newsletter I give an introduction to the latest few posts and occasionally give some additional commentary. In my latest newsletter I wrote

Projective space and homogeneous coordinates seemed like arbitrary abstractions when I was a student because they were presented without any motivation. Much later I came to realize that they’re natural, almost inevitable. Exceptional cases and hand-wavy references to objects “at infinity” go away when moving to projective space.

My mathematics education was very top-down: abstractions first, specifics later (if ever). I was OK with that for a while, until I hit my abstraction tolerance sometime in grad school. Now I would advocate more of a bottom-up approach, motivating abstractions first rather than presenting them as a fait acompli.

The first time I saw the projective plane was probably in a topology class where someone said you could construct the plane by starting with a square and gluing opposite edges in a physically impossible way. This seemed like a gimmick, a way to construct a non-orientable manifold but not anything practical. Another construction is to say the projective plane is an ordinary sphere with antipodal points identified. I found that a little more satisfying, but it still unmotivated.

What I would have appreciated was someone saying that the projective plane was invented to make geometry more elegant by eliminating exceptional cases and making rigorous the idea of things “at infinity.” For example, geometric calculations often have to treat vertical lines specially, but vertical lines are not special in projective geometry.

You could start by saying we’re going to represent points in the plane not simply as (x, y) but as (x, y, 1) and use (x, y, 0) for the point at infinity in the direction (x, y). That may seem like a hack, but it’s certainly motivated. It’s exactly the sort of thing a graphics programmer would do. In fact, I imagine many programmers have done just that, independently bumping into projective geometry.

After having introduced this extra coordinate, it’s natural to ask what would it mean if the last coordinate were something other than 0 or 1. You’ll quickly run into this when you start doing calculations on these extended coordinates. You could have a rule that you always normalize by dividing by the last coordinate, if it’s not zero, and then you have essentially discovered homogeneous coordinates.

You’ll see something like the approach above in elliptic curve cryptography. Programmers wanting to implement encryption algorithms are thinking concretely in terms of (x, y) points, until they have to worry about a mysterious “point at infinity” and handle it correctly. Then homogenous coordinates appear as a tool for getting out of a bind.

***

I thought about titling this post something like “Dr. Stragelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and and Love the Projective Plane” but I wasn’t sure how well that would go over. I doubt many readers have seen the 1964 movie this is alluding to, but the trope “How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love …” is more widely known than the movie itself.

entry.title: Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal
entry.content:
The Windows 2000 launch in San Francisco was accompanied by an expo, and a large number of Windows 2000 team members were dispatched to run the various booths and stations, give informal presentations on the new features of Windows 2000, and answer technical questions from the various attendees. And from among the people who were sent to the expo, a smaller group was selected to attend the launch event itself in person.

Related reading: A ticket to the Windows 95 launch.

After a few of us arrived early at the Civic Auditorium for the launch event, we had to entertain ourselves until the doors opened. There was some speculation as to who the celebrity host would be, since it hadn’t been announced. One of my colleagues tried to sneak into what looked like a VIP tent.¹ I, on the other hand, went exploring.

I found an unlocked door that took me into the empty upper level of the main auditorium.

I took a seat and tried not to be noticed.

The stage was set up with a 10-meter tall mock laptop, screens to the left and right of the stage for projecting slides, prerecorded videos, or to get a better look at on-stage close-ups, gray curtains unobtrusively hung to shield from view what would turn out to be various surprises throughout the event, and various other desks, demo areas, and even an airplane cabin set.²

While I sat and took in the complexity of the stage, there was an announcement that they would be rehearsing the opening in one minute. The lights dimmed in preparation. The lid of the giant laptop closed very slowly.

About ten minutes after the announcement, the rehearsal actually began.

The laptop lid opened, and on the laptop screen, it looked like someone was signing into Windows 2000, and then the mouse clicked the Start button. This led to a video montage, and when the montage was over, a voice announced, “Ladies and Gentlemen, please welcome Patrick Stewart!”

Oh my goodness, Patrick Stewart is going to be the presenter for the Windows 2000 launch!

Mere seconds later, onto the stage bounded… a crew member wearing a headset pretending to be Patrick Stewart so that the camera and lighting crew could make sure they were properly positioned.

Okay, that’s the end of the rehearsal. The lights come back on, and the auditorium once again buzzes with the sound of equipment being moved and people discussing things.

I left the auditorium and went back to join the crowd of people waiting to get in. I didn’t tell them who the host was.

The event itself seemed to go off pretty much as planned. With the real Patrick Stewart.

Patrick Stewart had such a commanding presence. If he had come out on stage and announced, “It is the dawn of a new era: The era of lime Jell-O”, people would say, “Yeah, lime Jell-O, I need to upgrade to lime Jell-O.” But instead of trying to spark a new dessert trend, he talked about Windows 2000, reading words from a teleprompter that he almost certainly didn’t understand, but he made them sound great.

¹ My colleague eventually returned with a Commemorative Edition boxed copy of Windows 2000.

² The airplane cabin was used for a sketch that demonstrated mobile business computing. The demoer took their laptop on a plane trip, where they happened to sit next to a character named William Wentworth, portrayed by actor John O’Hurley, president of William Wentworth Worldwide. (He gave his email address as www@www.com.) The sketch demonstrated infrared file sharing and other mobile scenarios. Remember infrared file sharing? Of course you don’t.

entry.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
entry.content:
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.

In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

Trained on Astra’s answer (& confidence), two attempts Copying heads Astra names (layer.head) Copying heads, ground truth Python Python (0.56), Python (0.52) 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 Romaji romaji (0.55), romaji (0.62) 3.3 3.3 English English (0.58), English (0.48) 3.1 3.1

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.

So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.

We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck.

We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.

From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.

Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.

We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network.

Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.

Game PPO, 100M steps PPO, 500M steps Astra, one-shot Breakout 15.8 25.3 517.4 Seaquest 5.6 88.9 53.1 Asterix 25.8 55.2 53.2

How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.

So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.

From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.

We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.

Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.

We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.

With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games.

How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more.

Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly.

We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA datasetThe QA dataset: GitHub.. One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning.

Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained.

It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion (Figure 2).

Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights.

We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed.

As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.

With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 (%) GSM8K (%) IFEval (%) Hit token limit (%) Base 7.9 13.8 21.0 93.0 Edited, 10 forward passes 12.3 25.7 49.0 87.2 Edited, 25 forward passes 14.1 25.1 39.9 86.4 Edited, 50 forward passes 48.1 67.1 62.3 33.1

Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.

Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.

Gemma 3 270M MATH-500 (%) Base 6.8 Edited, 5 forward passes 7.0 Edited, 10 forward passes 7.6 Edited, 25 forward passes 7.7 Edited, 50 forward passes 7.0

Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.

Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .

On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.

In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.

This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:

We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.

We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number.

entry.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
entry.content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security

[Submitted on 27 Oct 2026]

Title:Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining PoisoningView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. entry.title: SOML – A Config Format for Humans
entry.content:
A config format for humans SOML is short for Sindre's Objectively Marvelous Language.

SOML is a config format that is pleasant to write and easy to read. The top level needs no braces, keys need no quotes, line breaks replace commas, and comments go almost anywhere. A value's type comes from its syntax, never from its content, so what you see is what you get: '123' is a string and 123 is an int. Dates like 2026-09-19, instants like 2026-09-19T14:00:00Z, and durations like 30s are real values, so nobody has to guess the unit of timeout: 30. Paths and regexes need no escaping, and prose goes in block strings. One canonical form and a shared conformance suite mean every implementation reads your file the same way. JSON has the strictness but not the comfort: quotes, commas, and braces everywhere, and no comments. YAML has the comfort but not the clarity: - list markers, nested indentation, and types guessed from content, so country: no becomes false and version: 3.10 becomes 3.1. SOML gives you the comfort and the strictness, without the guessing.

Warning

Draft spec. Feedback welcome.

name: 'api-gateway' port: 8080 # The load balancer expects this port. timeout: 30s launch-date: 2027-09-19 windows-path: 'C:\Users\sindre\dev' description: ''' Terminates TLS. Routes requests to internal services. ''' allowed-origins: [ 'https://example.com' 'https://example.org' ]

The same in JSON:

{ "name": "api-gateway", "port": 8080, "timeout": 30, "launch-date": "2027-09-19", "windows-path": "C:\\Users\\sindre\\dev", "description": "Terminates TLS.\nRoutes requests to internal services.", "allowed-origins": [ "https://example.com", "https://example.org" ] }

SOML is a data format for files that people write and read. It is JSON without the noise, and with comments. It keeps JSON's tree of objects and arrays and its strictness, and adds literal strings, block strings, dates, instants, and durations.

Its design rests on one rule: a value's type comes from its syntax, never from its content. '123' is a string and 123 is an int. Nothing is ever retyped by inspecting it.

Less noise than JSON, and comments. Keys need no quotes, even with dashes, a line break replaces a comma, and the top level needs no braces. Comments are allowed wherever whitespace may go. What you see is the type. A string always has quotes, and a value without quotes must be a number, a date, an instant, a duration, or a keyword, or the file has an error. So country: no is an error rather than false, and '10.20' and 10.20 are a string and a float, exactly as written. Strict where JSON is vague. Duplicate keys, lone surrogates, and numbers out of range are errors, not behavior that each parser decides. An int is exact to 64 bits, and 3 and 3.0 stay different types. Pleasant to write. Literal strings, so paths and regexes need no escaping, and dedented block strings for prose. Dates, instants, and durations are values. 2026-09-19 is a calendar date, 2026-09-19T14:00:00Z is an instant, and 1h30m is a duration, so no reader has to parse a string or guess a unit. Indentation is free. Braces and line breaks give the structure, so tabs, spaces, and copy and paste never change what a file means, except inside a block string, where indentation is text. One canonical form. Equal values give equal bytes, for hashing, signing, and comparing. A separate formatter keeps your comments, member order, and the spelling of each value. Its rules are part of the spec, so every conforming formatter gives the same output for the same file. Small and tested. The grammar is one pass with no lookahead, and every implementation runs the language-neutral conformance suite of nearly 1000 cases, so every implementation reads a file the same way. /* Everything SOML can express, in one document. A document may also be a top-level array. */ # Keys are bare. Dashes are allowed, so no key needs quotes. name: 'soml' launch-date: 2027-09-19 released-at: 2026-09-19T14:00:00Z 'the name': 'quotes are the escape hatch, when a key needs spaces' 404: 'and a key may begin with a digit' # Strings: '...' is literal, "..." is escaped. Use ' by default. regex: '^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$' windows-path: 'C:\Users\sindre\dev' shell: 'echo "$HOME" | tr -d "\n"' escaped: "line one\nline two\t\"quoted\"\u{1f600}" # Block strings are dedented by the closing delimiter's column. description: ''' A block string keeps its line breaks. The leading tab of each line is stripped, because the closing delimiter sits at one tab. ''' # Numbers: int and float are different types. replicas: 3 ratio: 0.75 budget: 1_000_000 mask: 0b1010_1100 permissions: 0o644 color: 0xFF8800 flags: 0x00FF limit: infinity floor: -infinity # Booleans and null. drained: false owner: null # Durations: exact, in h, m, s, ms, us, and ns. retry-after: 1m30s # Arrays. A comma or a line break separates items. labels: ['prod', 'eu-west', 'canary'] matrix: [[1, 2], [3, 4]] mixed: [1, 'two', true, null] # Objects. The top-level object needs no braces. pool: { min: 2 max: 16 } # Records in arrays. Braces are required, and that is deliberate. maintainers: [ {name: 'Sindre Sorhus', email: 'sindresorhus@gmail.com'} {name: 'Random Person', email: 'person@example.com'} ] # Line comments, and block comments, wherever whitespace may go. # Inline objects and one-line braced documents work too: healthcheck: {path: '/health', interval: 10s, grace: 1.5s}

SOML keeps what I like about YAML: comments, no braces around the file, no commas at the ends of lines, and keys without quotes. It removes what hurts: in YAML, the content of a value decides its type. In SOML, the syntax decides, so 'no' is a string, 3.10 is a float, and 2 is an int, in every implementation.

What SOML adds:

Block comments with /* */, in addition to #. Durations such as 30s and 1h30m, so timeout: 30 no longer makes the reader guess the unit. Dates such as 2026-09-19 and instants such as 2026-09-19T14:00:00Z. YAML 1.2 dropped timestamps, but many parsers still read them, so a date in YAML may or may not be a string. A canonical form, so equal values give equal bytes for hashing and signing. YAML defines one for scalars only. A formatter whose rules are part of the spec. It keeps your comments, key order, and the spelling of each value. YAML says comments are not content, so tools may drop them. Editing rules, so a tool can change one value and keep the comments and layout of the rest. Error messages that usually say what to write instead.

What SOML fixes:

Values change type without warning. In PyYAML (YAML 1.1), country: no is false, zip: 01234 is octal 668, and time: 22:22 is base-60 1342. YAML 1.2 fixed those, but most of the ecosystem still follows 1.1, and 1.2 still guesses: version: 3.10 is the float 3.1, and ~, Null, and an empty value are null. SOML strings always have quotes, so country: no is an error. Keys are not always strings. 1: x gives an integer key in YAML, and PyYAML reads on: x as the boolean true. SOML keys are always strings, so 404: is the key '404'. Indentation is the structure. One space too few moves a key into another object, and the file still parses, which is why YAML forbids tabs there. SOML gets its structure from braces and line breaks, so indentation only helps the reader, except in a block string, where it is text. Block strings add a newline. YAML's default | keeps a trailing \n in the value; SOML does not. Large ints lose precision. js-yaml turns id: 9007199254740993 into 9007199254740992. A SOML int is an exact int64; a larger one is an error. Duplicate keys go unnoticed. For a: 1 then a: 2, PyYAML keeps 2 and says nothing. The spec forbids duplicates, but after type resolution 1: and 01: may or may not collide, depending on the schema. SOML compares the decoded strings and reports each duplicate. A missing value is null. timeout: with no value is null in YAML, and a file with only comments is null in PyYAML. SOML rejects both, so a forgotten value cannot pass as a default. The language is large. YAML has two syntaxes for every list and map, two block string styles with three newline rules, indentation indicators, anchors, aliases, tags, multiple documents per file, three processing stages, and three recommended schemas. SOML has one syntax for each, one block string style, and one set of type rules. Parsers disagree. In the YAML test matrix (newest snapshot 2022), PyYAML fails 73 of 402 cases. 2024-01-01 is a date in PyYAML and a string in js-yaml 5, and 1_000 is 1000 in PyYAML and a string in js-yaml. SOML implementations share one conformance suite of nearly 1000 cases. Two features are a security risk. Aliases make YAML bombs possible: a small file expands into billions of nodes. Tags let a loader construct objects, and PyYAML has had four remote code execution CVEs rated 9.8. safe_load is opt-in, and even a loader named “safe” can turn aliases on. SOML has neither, one way to load, and limits on nesting and ranges.

SOML keeps what TOML gets right: predictable types, literal strings, insignificant indentation, and duplicate keys as errors. It removes what hurts: table rules where a key's meaning depends on what came before it, and values that parsers silently round, truncate, or read differently. A SOML file means one thing, no matter where a line sits or which parser reads it.

What SOML adds:

Top-level arrays. A TOML file is always a table, so a list of records needs a wrapper key. Block comments with /* */, in addition to #. Line breaks in place of commas, so a multi-line array needs none. Durations such as 30s and 1h30m, so timeout = 30 no longer makes the reader guess the unit. A calendar date and an instant, kept as distinct types, without local date-times or local times. A canonical form, so equal values give equal bytes for hashing and signing. A formatter whose rules are part of the spec, so every conforming formatter gives the same output.

What SOML fixes:

Three ways to nest. [server] with port = 8080, server.port = 8080, and server = {port = 8080} all give the same table, each with its own rules. Projects mix them, often in one file. SOML has one way: braces. Later lines can change earlier tables. Even at the end of a file, [[users]] adds to an earlier array, [server.tls] to an earlier table, and a bare key to the last table. An attacker who can put a newline into one value can add a user with role = 'admin', as CVE-2026-44244 injected a [core] section into .git/config for code execution. BurntSushi/toml even lets a later users = ['mallory'] under [auth] silently replace an earlier [auth.users.alice] table. In SOML, earlier objects and arrays are closed. Table headers have hidden scope. [server] moves every following key into server, even timeout = 30, with no way back to the root. SOML braces make boundaries explicit. Dotted paths behave differently from headers. Inside [server], logging.level = 'debug' is server.logging.level, but [logging] is a root table, and server.port = 8080 is server.server.port. In SOML, a key belongs to the braces around it. Extension rules depend on how a table was made. [a.b] then [a] is valid, but a.b.c = 1 then [a] is not. Header and dotted-key tables can be extended, inline tables cannot, and [[servers]] can append to an array of tables, but not to servers = []. SOML has no implicit tables, and one syntax each for objects and arrays. Arrays of tables depend on order. [servers.tls] attaches to the most recent [[servers]], so moving a section can silently attach it to another server. SOML array elements are self-contained objects. Dotted keys silently change structure. 3.14 = 'pi', example.com, and tls.crt are nested keys, and servers.0.port creates the key '0', not an array element. SOML needs quotes for a literal dot. Renaming requires chasing paths. Headers such as [server.database] and [server.cache] repeat the parent name, so a rename that misses one silently creates a separate object. SOML names the parent once. Reindentation changes strings. Multiline strings keep their indentation and the newline before the closing delimiter, and newline normalization is platform-dependent. SOML dedents block strings, adds no trailing newline, and requires LF. No null, but nan. TOML cannot tell an explicit null from a missing key, so writers must drop it or fail: @iarna/toml silently drops a null value, and Python's toml turns None in an array into the string 'None'. TOML has nan. SOML has null, and no nan, which is not equal to itself. Numbers and times change between parsers. 1e999 is infinity in Python's tomllib and smol-toml, but an error in Go and Rust, and 1e-400 is zero in all of them. .123456789 seconds is exact in Go and Rust, .123456 in tomllib, and .123 in smol-toml. 9223372036854775808 works in tomllib but not in Rust's toml. SOML ints are exact int64, instants keep nanoseconds, and a float that does not fit is an error. Broken input passes. TOML reads an empty or comment-only file as an empty table, permits replacing malformed UTF-8 with U+FFFD, and leaves BOM handling unspecified. SOML rejects all of these, so an emptied config cannot fall back to defaults. JSON must be rewritten. TOML uses =, so a JSON object cannot be pasted in, not even as a value. SOML uses :, so hand-written JSON is usually valid SOML, and the syntax is already familiar from JSON, YAML, and JavaScript.

JSON is unambiguous but noisy to write: the file needs braces around it, every item needs a comma, every key needs quotes, and there are no comments. YAML is pleasant to write but ambiguous to read. SOML keeps JSON's data model and strictness, and also decides what JSON leaves to each implementation. From YAML, it takes comments, multi-line strings, and a top level with no braces or commas, but not implicit typing, significant indentation, aliases, or tags. From TOML, it takes literal strings and the split between int and float, but it allows a top-level array and has no table headers or dotted keys.

SOML JSON YAML 1.2 TOML 1.1 Comments # and /* */ no # # Braces around a top-level object no required no no Commas between items on separate lines no required no required in arrays and inline tables Keys without quotes yes, dashes and digits included no yes yes A value's type comes from its syntax yes yes no, an unquoted value is typed by its content yes Separate int and float yes no yes yes Dates and durations date, instant, and duration no no, but many parsers still read dates four date and time types, no duration Duplicate keys an error left to the parser an error, but some parsers keep the last an error A top-level array yes yes yes no Indentation changes the meaning no no yes no Canonical form yes only in a separate scheme, RFC 8785 for scalars only no Libraries new, in a few languages everywhere everywhere most languages

See the full comparison with JSON, JSON5, JSONC, TOML, YAML, and other formats, including where another format is the better choice.

The format is defined in the specification, which also gives the reason for each decision. The FAQ gives short answers to common questions, such as why SOML has durations and separate int and float types.
